FIGHTER MOVEMENT — ZIGZAGS AND COVER, THIS GOVERNS EVERY FIGHTER IN EVERY BEAT: nobody runs at the building and nobody runs in a straight line. Every rush is THREE TO FIVE PACES, bent low, CHANGING DIRECTION TWO OR THREE TIMES INSIDE THAT SINGLE RUSH — cutting left, then right, then left again — and ending with the man going DOWN hard behind the next piece of cover, flat or on one knee, weapon coming up over it. They come OUT OF THE ALLEY MOUTHS ONE AT A TIME, and the first thing each man does on breaking cover is cut diagonally instead of running up the lane. They stop behind the ENGINE BLOCK AND WHEELS of the wrecked cars, never the doors. They CUT THE CORNERS OF THE BUILDINGS TIGHT, shoulder almost scraping the render, muzzle leading, one fast look and gone. They hug the base of walls in the shadow. They go through the gap in the low wall on their bellies one at a time and move along the drainage ditch on elbows and knees. They cross open ground ONE MAN AT A TIME on the diagonal. They move IN PAIRS, BOUNDING — one up and moving while the other is down covering, then swapping, never both moving at once. AND AT EVERY STOP AT LEAST ONE OF THEM SNAPS HIS HEAD UP AT THE ROOFLINE of the corner house, because they know there are snipers on it and it visibly decides where they choose to stop. Weapons in the shoulder or held high across the body while moving, never dangling.

HOW HITS ARE SHOWN: a man who is hit STOPS WORKING AND GOES DOWN — the read is the sudden loss of intention, a rush that ends mid-stride, a body that drops instead of falls, a weapon released. Dust and torn cloth fibres puff off the impact point, the body twists away from it, and there is no next move. NO BLOOD, NO WOUNDS, NO GORE, NO RED MIST. Enemy casualties always at DISTANCE and small in frame.

7-10s | THE WINDOW. WIDE, LOW, FROM INSIDE THE GROUND-FLOOR ROOM looking out through a sandbagged window hole: a SEAL is standing at the window hole firing his carbine out into the lane, helmet on, goggles down over his eyes, brass flicking off to one side, sandbags bursting and pouring beside him as rounds come in. AND HE IS HIT. He stops firing mid-burst, comes off the weapon, and goes straight down out of the frame below the sill — the carbine dropping with him. THAT IS THE WHOLE BEAT. 10-14s | SLOW MOTION — JACK IS HIT. Tight, close, low behind the parapet, EXTREME SLOW MOTION, all of it read on him and his kit: <<<93edeb87-e0e7-4ded-9569-527aca55e457>>> is up on his elbows on the rifle when the round arrives in his RIGHT SHOULDER. The impact goes through his body before his face knows about it — the shoulder is driven violently backwards and down, dust and a small burst of torn cloth fibres puff off the top of the shoulder where it strikes, the plate carrier strap snaps taut and jumps, his helmet whips over with the rotation of the torso and the goggle strap pulls tight across the cover. The rifle comes off the bipod and out of his hands, the bolt handle catching the concrete. His right arm goes dead and swings loose. He lands on his side against the parapet with his cheek on the grit, mouth open, breath driven out of him, and for a full beat he does nothing at all — the blankness of a body switched off and switched back on. His eyes stay visible behind the dusty scratched lens the whole time. No blood, no wound, no hole. Empty brass and grit float and turn in the slowed air around him.

He does not look at Terrence, not at the lane, not at the lens. He examines it the way you examine something that belongs to someone else, breathing hard the whole time.

SECOND — THE REACTION ARRIVES IN HIS BODY (about two seconds, no words at all), involuntary and physical, not acted: a sharp shallow catch of breath sucked in through the teeth; the head tips BACK against the concrete and the eyes screw shut hard behind the lens; the jaw clamps; HIS LEFT HAND COMES ACROSS AND PRESSES FLAT OVER THE SHOULDER AND STAYS THERE; his breathing goes short, fast and shallow through the nose, chest lifting; a shudder runs through him once. He rides it out.

THIRD — THE WORD (about one and a half seconds). The worst of it passes through him, his head comes back down off the wall, his eyes open behind the lens, and he says it on an out-breath — flat, quiet, tired, disgusted, half under his breath, not a shout:
JACK: "Shit!"

FOURTH — THE HAND MOVES, STILL THE SAME SHOT AND THE SAME POSITION, AND THIS IS THE HINGE OF THE TAKE: the LEFT hand — the same hand that has been pressing his shoulder — LIFTS OFF THE WOUND and travels up to the shoulder mic clipped on the left strap of his plate carrier. We see it leave the shoulder and we see it close on the mic. He does not use the right arm, which stays dead and hanging. He does not change how he is lying. The camera stays exactly where it is and simply lets his hand come up into frame. He squeezes the transmit key and takes ONE DEEP RAGGED BREATH before he speaks, and we hear it.

FIFTH — THE RADIO CALL (six full seconds for eighteen words, same unbroken shot, same position, left hand on the mic at his collarbone the whole time). HE IS SHOUTING AND HE IS OUT OF BREATH AT THE SAME TIME, AND THE BREATHLESSNESS IS AS IMPORTANT AS THE VOLUME. Loud, raised, forced, hoarse, straining over the volume of the firefight — but there is not enough air behind it. Each phrase is HAMMERED OUT ON WHATEVER AIR HE HAS, and then he RUNS OUT and has to STOP AND DRAG IN A LOUD RAGGED BREATH THROUGH HIS MOUTH before he can start the next one. The breaths are audible, deep, wet and uneven, and they are what create the gaps between phrases. His voice cracks and thins on the loudest words because it is being pushed past what his lungs have. Real emotion under it: fury and urgency, teeth showing, the cords standing out in his neck.
AND ADRENALINE IS SLOWING HIM DOWN — his brain is a half-beat behind his mouth. Before some phrases there is a small blank hesitation, a beat too long, as if he has to find the next words; once he almost starts a word, stops, drags a breath, and starts it again; the repetition of SURROUNDED comes out because for a second he has genuinely lost the thread and falls back on the drill. He is not sharp, he is running on chemistry — heavy, hoarse, half a step behind, and hammering it out anyway.
HE STILL DOES NOT GABBLE, DOES NOT RUSH AND DOES NOT RUN THE PHRASES TOGETHER. Every word fully formed and hit hard, nothing swallowed, nothing crammed. Loud, breathless and slow at the same time.
JACK (shouting into the radio, hoarse and badly out of breath, one short phrase at a time, dragging a loud ragged breath between each, a half-beat behind himself):
"All stations! — this is Reaper! — We are SURROUNDED! — I say again — SURROUNDED! — We need air support — NOW!"
Behind him, out of focus in the same frame, <<<4f969abd-60d2-4e34-9da2-d933f91e3688>>> is back down on his rifle and firing.

RADIO (male, calm, American): "Copy, Reaper. Hawk is inbound. Hang tight, boys."
His hand comes off the mic and drops back onto the shoulder. He closes his eyes for half a second behind the lens, breathing still ragged, and that is the only thing his face does. Hold. Last frame.

ACTING TASK — JACK: he is triaging, not suffering. When he looks at the shoulder he is checking a piece of equipment. The reaction that follows is his body overruling him for two seconds, and he lets it pass through rather than fighting it or performing it. "Shit" is irritation at a tool that broke, said quietly because there is nobody he wants to say it to. THEN THE RADIO CALL IS THE OPPOSITE — this is the one moment in the film where he loses his temper, because he has one arm, a man down at the window and forty men closing, and the only thing left that can change the outcome is at the other end of that radio. He is not asking, he is DEMANDING, at full volume. But his body will not cooperate: no air, hands shaking, adrenaline making him half a beat slow, so every phrase costs him a breath and he has to stop and take it. He forces the words out separated and complete anyway, because a man who cannot be understood gets nothing. To make the call he takes the pressure off his own wound and does not hesitate about it for a moment.
ACTING TASK — TERRENCE: for two seconds he stops being a soldier entirely. He is not assessing a casualty and he is not looking for a threat — he is looking AT JACK, the man at his right elbow, and there is nothing else in his eyeline or in his head. Then he puts himself back together and goes back on the gun, and the effort of doing it is visible on him.
ACTING TASK — THE FIGHTERS: not suicidal and not extras. Every man is trying to get thirty metres closer without being the next one down — zigzag rushes, proper cover, heads up at the roofline at every stop; when the man beside them goes down they do not stop, they change their line.

SOUND: two bolt-actions and carbines working, AK fire from four directions cracking off concrete, rounds hitting sandbags and stone, brass on the deck, Pashto passed lane to lane. Under the SLOW MOTION beat the mix drops to a muffled underwater roar with the impact itself almost dry and small, then a thin ringing. Normal speed returns with Terrence's shout. FROM 16s TO THE LAST FRAME JACK'S BREATHING IS MIXED LOUD AND CLOSE ON THE MIC AND NEVER STOPS — hard ragged mouth-breathing, hitches and catches, the deep dragged breath before every radio phrase, and the heaving after the call; it is the second loudest thing in the scene after his shouting. It gets worse across the take, not better. Everything below happens inside this one frame, in this order.

FIRST — HE LOOKS (about two seconds). His head comes down and he LOOKS AT HIS OWN RIGHT SHOULDER, at the torn dusty fabric where the round went in. He does not look at Terrence, not at the lane, not at the lens. He examines it the way you examine something that belongs to someone else, breathing hard the whole time.

SECOND — THE REACTION ARRIVES IN HIS BODY (about two seconds, no words at all), involuntary and physical, not acted: a sharp shallow catch of breath sucked in through the teeth; the head tips BACK against the concrete and the eyes screw shut hard behind the lens; the jaw clamps; HIS LEFT HAND COMES ACROSS AND PRESSES FLAT OVER THE SHOULDER AND STAYS THERE; his breathing goes short, fast and shallow through the nose, chest lifting; a shudder runs through him once. He rides it out.

THIRD — THE WORD (about one second). The worst of it passes through him, his head comes back down off the wall, his eyes open behind the lens, and he says it on an out-breath — flat, quiet, tired, disgusted, half under his breath, not a shout:
JACK: "Shit!"

FOURTH — THE HAND MOVES, STILL THE SAME SHOT AND THE SAME POSITION, AND THIS IS THE HINGE OF THE TAKE (about one and a half seconds): the LEFT hand — the same hand that has been pressing his shoulder — LIFTS OFF THE WOUND and travels up to the shoulder mic clipped on the left strap of his plate carrier. We see it leave the shoulder and we see it close on the mic. He does not use the right arm, which stays dead and hanging. He does not change how he is lying. The camera stays exactly where it is and simply lets his hand come up into frame. He squeezes the transmit key and takes ONE DEEP RAGGED BREATH before he speaks, and we hear it.

FIFTH — THE RADIO CALL (six full seconds for eighteen words, same unbroken shot, same position, left hand on the mic at his collarbone the whole time). HE IS SHOUTING AND HE IS OUT OF BREATH AT THE SAME TIME, AND THE BREATHLESSNESS IS AS IMPORTANT AS THE VOLUME. Loud, raised, forced, hoarse, straining over the volume of the firefight — but there is not enough air behind it. Each phrase is HAMMERED OUT ON WHATEVER AIR HE HAS, and then he RUNS OUT and has to STOP AND DRAG IN A LOUD RAGGED BREATH THROUGH HIS MOUTH before he can start the next one. The breaths are audible, deep and uneven, and they are what create the gaps between phrases. His voice cracks and thins on the loudest words because it is being pushed past what his lungs have. Fury and urgency under it: teeth showing, the cords standing out in his neck.
BUT THE WORDS THEMSELVES ARE CORRECT, CLEAN AND COMPLETE RADIO PROCEDURE — he never stumbles, never loses the thread, never repeats himself, never mumbles and never says anything unclear. Every word fully formed and hit hard, nothing swallowed, nothing crammed. Loud, breathless and slow at the same time.
JACK (shouting into the radio, hoarse and badly out of breath, one short phrase at a time, dragging a loud ragged breath between each):
"All stations, this is Reaper! — We are surrounded! — Taking fire from all four sides! — We need close air support — NOW!"
Behind him, out of focus in the same frame, <<<4f969abd-60d2-4e34-9da2-d933f91e3688>>> is down on his rifle and firing.

SIXTH — THE ANSWER (the last two seconds, still the same unbroken shot, same position, left hand still on the mic): hold on his face, chest heaving, still fighting for air, as the radio comes back — thin, compressed and crackling out of a speaker, and by contrast completely calm, unhurried and clearly enunciated:
RADIO (male, calm, American): "Copy, Reaper. Hawk is inbound. Hang tight, boys."
His hand comes off the mic and drops back onto the shoulder. He closes his eyes for half a second behind the lens, breathing still ragged, and that is the only thing his face does. Hold. Last frame.

ACTING TASK — JACK: he is triaging, not suffering. When he looks at the shoulder he is checking a piece of equipment. The reaction that follows is his body overruling him for two seconds, and he lets it pass through rather than fighting it or performing it. "Shit" is irritation at a tool that broke, said quietly because there is nobody he wants to say it to. THEN THE RADIO CALL IS THE OPPOSITE — this is the one moment in the film where he loses his temper, because he has one arm, a man down at the window and forty men closing, and the only thing left that can change the outcome is at the other end of that radio. He is not asking, he is DEMANDING, at full volume. But his body will not cooperate: no air, so every phrase costs him a breath and he has to stop and take it. The words stay correct and procedural anyway, because a man who cannot be understood gets nothing. To make the call he takes the pressure off his own wound and does not hesitate about it for a moment.
ACTING TASK — TERRENCE: for two seconds he stops being a soldier entirely — he is not assessing a casualty and he is not looking for a threat, he is looking at his friend and he is going to him without thinking about it. The burst into the wall is what makes the decision for him, not judgement: his body flinches flat before his mind catches up, and when it does catch up he understands that crossing two feet of concrete will kill him and Jack both. Going back on the rifle is not him recovering his professionalism, it is him giving something up, and the last look he throws at Jack before he does it is the cost.
ACTING TASK — THE FIGHTERS: not suicidal and not extras. Every man is trying to get thirty metres closer without being the next one down — zigzag rushes, proper cover, heads up at the roofline at every stop; when the man beside them goes down they do not stop, they change their line.

SOUND: two bolt-actions and carbines working, AK fire from four directions cracking off concrete, rounds hitting sandbags and stone, brass on the deck, Pashto passed lane to lane. Under the SLOW MOTION beat the mix drops to a muffled underwater roar with the impact itself almost dry and small, then a thin ringing. Normal speed returns with Terrence's shout. The burst into the parapet beside him is four hard cracks and the spatter of concrete chips, very close on the mic. FROM 15.5s TO THE LAST FRAME JACK'S BREATHING IS MIXED LOUD AND CLOSE AND NEVER STOPS — hard ragged mouth-breathing, hitches and catches, the deep dragged breath before every radio phrase, and the heaving after the call. The radio reply is thin, compressed and crackling out of a speaker, calm and perfectly intelligible against him. No music.

杰克与特伦斯是一队美军:统一美军沙漠迷彩、头盔、防弹背心,并肩一处,朝同一方向——巷子另一侧——作战。杰克是精确射手,特伦斯是他的掩护。敌人是伏击的武装分子:便装、缠头巾、无制服无头盔,躲在对面土墙后、屋顶、巷口开火。杰克与特伦斯从不互相射击——他们是一对搭档,共同对抗便装武装分子。
【SCENE / 场景】
战争闪回,阿富汗白天。杰克架枪在一处高点(半塌土楼的窗口),特伦斯贴身掩护;一支美军小队在下方土坯村庄突遭武装分子伏击。烈日、尘土、硝烟。整段是被创伤扭曲的记忆:模糊、抽格、耳鸣。由当下的四声枪响引爆。
【ACTION / 动作】22秒,动作语法,机枪般急切
引爆(0–2秒):快特写——杰克(美军军服头盔)贴着精确射手步枪的瞄准镜向前射击,枪口频闪照亮沾尘的脸。四声急促枪响,每次闪光撕开一格过去:白色天空/奔跑军靴/无声张嘴/——第四声,声音塌成耳鸣,已在战争里。
伏击爆发(2–6秒):爆炸性混乱,每格0.4至0.6秒,全带失焦色差晕影:巷子另一侧,缠头巾的便装武装分子从土墙后与屋顶开火,枪口火光在对面频闪;高点上,杰克据枪精确点射,弹壳弹出机匣旋落;身旁特伦斯半跪着朝侧翼短点射,替杰克挡住来袭方向,回头对他吼了句被耳鸣吞掉的话。清晰的两侧对抗。
狙击与掩护(6–11秒):正反打的急切节奏——杰克瞄准镜里,对面屋顶一个武装分子的身影被击中旋身翻倒出视野(只在动作中一闪,不给特写);特伦斯一把按住杰克的背心把他往窗侧一拽,一发流弹恰打碎他们头顶的土墙,碎土飞溅;两人重新据枪。他们像一台咬合的机器,一个射击一个掩护。
位置被打崩·特伦斯拖救(11–15秒):对面一波集火砸上他们的窗口,土墙成片炸裂,杰克被气浪掀得踉跄失衡、几乎从高点栽下。特伦斯一把抓住杰克的背心,把他整个人从暴露的窗口拖回掩体后——一边拖一边朝武装分子方向短点射压制。尘烟里那个宽肩身影死死拽住杰克不放。(观众此刻认不出这名搭档是谁。)
孩子(15–20秒,核心,骤然切入慢镜):杰克重新架枪、扣住扳机的那条火线前方 <<<image_3>>> ——几个阿富汗孩子突然从横巷冲出,穿过战场奔逃,慢动作,尘埃在他们周围悬浮,惊恐的小脸、飞扬的衣角;杰克在瞄准镜里猛地看见他们——时间凝滞——他扣着扳机的手僵住,眼睛在镜片后骤然睁大,战斗机器的冷硬一瞬碎裂。定格在孩子奔跑的慢镜与他震裂的眼睛之间。这一刻是伤口:二十年后他会在窗前再次僵住,那扇窗、那副瞄准镜、那双眼睛,是同一个。
爆炸(20–22秒):慢镜猛地弹回实时——一团巨大爆炸在下方巷子炸开,白光尘土扑向镜头,冲击波掀翻画面——一记巨大次声波撞击穿透耳鸣——画面在撞击瞬间炸成全黑。保持黑。
【CAMERA / 摄影】
动作语法:超广角贴身手持,机位随身体加速与落定,荷兰角逐镜换向。伏击与狙击掩护段最急最抖;拖救段跟着特伦斯把杰克往后拽的重心;孩子段切入慢动作、机位略稳但晕影色差不减;爆炸回实时。全段地平线持续倾斜。特写瞄准镜时给圆形渐晕与分划线,但仍在动作语法的急促里。
【ACTING TASK — 杰克】
终身动机:训练把他磨成执行程序的精确射手,不许迟疑。
本场目标:从高点压制伏击、护住下方小队、和特伦斯守住这个位置。
障碍:火线前方突然冲出的孩子。
战术:整场他是冷硬的机器,眼睛只做测距、锁定、扣发;和特伦斯的配合是本能,不用看就知道对方在哪;直到瞄准镜里出现孩子,机器第一次卡死——这次卡死,和二十年后窗前那次,是同一双眼睛、同一副瞄准镜。
【ACTING TASK — 特伦斯】
终身动机:掩护搭档是他的本分,搭档的命比自己的重。
本场目标:替杰克挡住侧翼,位置一崩就把他拖出来。
战术:眼睛不停扫杰克的暴露面与侧翼威胁;位置被砸崩的瞬间,他一秒都不犹豫地抓住杰克往回拖——他一次都没松手。
安全线:双方视线始终投入任务,绝不呆滞;自然眨眼;唯杰克看见孩子的定格例外。
【SOUND】
当下四声枪响真实清脆;第四声起硬切进时时统治全段的高频耳鸣。伏击狙击:精确点射、弹壳落、特伦斯的短点射与被耳鸣吞掉的吼声、碎土飞溅、军靴。拖救段:粗重呼吸、拖拽摩擦、压制短射。孩子段骤然抽掉大部分声音,只余一条高音与孩子模糊脚步。最后爆炸一记巨大次声波撞击,然后死寂全黑。无音乐,无对白。
【FORBIDDEN / 禁止】
无血、无伤口、无尸体特写;美军之间绝不互相射击;武装分子中弹只在动作中一闪,不给定格特写;不表现瞄准镜十字与孩子在同一构图里对准锁定;无字幕、无音乐;地平线不得水平稳定。NO SCOPE POV

Duration: 30s. AFGHANISTAN, KABUL, DAY — the house is surrounded and Jack takes a round through the right shoulder. GRADE: warm GOLDEN Afghan daylight — honey-and-sand, creamy gold sun, dusty tan and khaki, 16mm grain, gentle halation, gold and dust. LENS: ANAMORPHIC 2.39:1, shallow focus, oval bokeh, horizontal smear. No starbursts, no flare streaks. Ground and roof shots violently unsteady and handheld — the frame lurches, the horizon rolls and never levels, pans overshoot and correct, focus is hunted by hand, impacts punch the image, grit on the glass. NORMAL SPEED EVERYWHERE except the one beat marked SLOW MOTION.

GEOGRAPHY: <<<image_5>>> the corner house — bare block walls, sandbagged window holes, one collapsed corner, a flat roof slab with a parapet. Four lanes running in from four directions, alley mouths, a burnt-out minibus on its rims, TWO WRECKED CARS, rubble mounds, a shallow concrete drainage ditch, courtyard walls with gates, a low wall with a gap in it, stacked breeze blocks. ON THE ROOF: <<<93edeb87-e0e7-4ded-9569-527aca55e457>>> and <<<4f969abd-60d2-4e34-9da2-d933f91e3688>>> lie side by side behind the parapet on their sand-coloured bolt-action sniper rifles on tan bipods, and two more SEALs along the deck with sand-coloured carbines. NO MACHINE GUN AND NO MACHINE GUNNER anywhere in this scene. Below, three SEALs at the sandbagged window holes with carbines.

THEIR POSITIONS ARE FIXED AND NEVER CHANGE, AND THE SCREEN GEOMETRY IS THIS: SEEN FROM THE FRONT, WITH THE CAMERA FACING THEM, <<<93edeb87-e0e7-4ded-9569-527aca55e457>>> IS ON THE LEFT SIDE OF FRAME AND <<<4f969abd-60d2-4e34-9da2-d933f91e3688>>> IS ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF FRAME. They lie shoulder to shoulder, less than an arm's length apart, both prone behind the same stretch of parapet facing the same way. When <<<4f969abd-60d2-4e34-9da2-d933f91e3688>>> turns his head to look at <<<93edeb87-e0e7-4ded-9569-527aca55e457>>>, ON SCREEN HIS HEAD TURNS TOWARD THE LEFT OF FRAME, to the man immediately beside him at ground level. Neither man is ever separated from the other, ever at the far end of the roof, or ever out of reach, and they never swap sides at any point in the scene.

HELMET AND EYEWEAR LOCK — DESCRIBED IN FULL, NOT BY REFERENCE, EVERY AMERICAN, EVERY BEAT: on the character reference sheets the helmet and the goggles are standing on the floor beside the figure — DO NOT COPY THAT. In this scene they are worn.
THE HELMET IS ON HIS HEAD: a modern military combat helmet in DESERT TAN with a dusty tan cloth cover, a night-vision mounting shroud and bracket on the front plate, accessory rails down both sides, a bungee cord across the top of the shell, an adjustable chinstrap FASTENED UNDER THE JAW with the cheek pads visible, the whole shell scuffed and grey with dust.
THE GOGGLES ARE DOWN OVER HIS EYES: a wide single-lens ballistic goggle sitting against the brow and the cheekbones, covering both eyes completely, held by a broad TAN ELASTIC STRAP that runs round the back of the helmet shell over the cover; the lens is clear-to-light-smoke, badly scratched, smeared and filmed with dust, and HIS EYES READ CLEARLY THROUGH IT — we can see the eyes, the lids, the lashes and where he is looking at all times.
<<<93edeb87-e0e7-4ded-9569-527aca55e457>>>: helmet on his head, goggles down over his eyes. <<<4f969abd-60d2-4e34-9da2-d933f91e3688>>>: helmet on his head, goggles down over his eyes. Every other American in frame: helmet on his head, goggles down over his eyes. IN EVERY BEAT AND EVERY CLOSE-UP. Nobody is bare-headed at any point, nobody removes a helmet, nobody pushes the goggles up onto the shell or onto the forehead, nobody wears them round the neck, and no helmet or goggles are ever lying on the ground.
THE REST OF THE KIT: tan plate carriers with three stacked magazine pouches and a shoulder radio with a whip antenna on the left strap, tan gloves, arid camo combat shirts with the sleeves rolled above the elbow and a subdued US flag patch on the right sleeve, trousers with built-in knee pads, a black pistol in a tan drop-leg holster on the right thigh, tan suede boots — everything dusty, sweat-stained, worn, never clean, never costume.

FIGHTER MOVEMENT — ZIGZAGS AND COVER, THIS GOVERNS EVERY FIGHTER IN EVERY BEAT: nobody runs at the building and nobody runs in a straight line. Every rush is THREE TO FIVE PACES, bent low, CHANGING DIRECTION TWO OR THREE TIMES INSIDE THAT SINGLE RUSH — cutting left, then right, then left again — and ending with the man going DOWN hard behind the next piece of cover, flat or on one knee, weapon coming up over it. They come OUT OF THE ALLEY MOUTHS ONE AT A TIME, and the first thing each man does on breaking cover is cut diagonally instead of running up the lane. They stop behind the ENGINE BLOCK AND WHEELS of the wrecked cars, never the doors. They CUT THE CORNERS OF THE BUILDINGS TIGHT, shoulder almost scraping the render, muzzle leading, one fast look and gone. They hug the base of walls in the shadow. They go through the gap in the low wall on their bellies one at a time and move along the drainage ditch on elbows and knees. They cross open ground ONE MAN AT A TIME on the diagonal. They move IN PAIRS, BOUNDING — one up and moving while the other is down covering, then swapping, never both moving at once. AND AT EVERY STOP AT LEAST ONE OF THEM SNAPS HIS HEAD UP AT THE ROOFLINE of the corner house, because they know there are snipers on it and it visibly decides where they choose to stop. Weapons in the shoulder or held high across the body while moving, never dangling.

HOW HITS ARE SHOWN: a man who is hit STOPS WORKING AND GOES DOWN — the read is the sudden loss of intention, a rush that ends mid-stride, a body that drops instead of falls, a weapon released. Dust and torn cloth fibres puff off the impact point, the body twists away from it, and there is no next move. NO BLOOD, NO WOUNDS, NO GORE, NO RED MIST. Enemy casualties always at DISTANCE and small in frame.

0-2.5s | ROOF, MEDIUM ON THE TWO OF THEM SIDE BY SIDE — JACK ON THE LEFT OF FRAME, TERRENCE ON THE RIGHT: <<<93edeb87-e0e7-4ded-9569-527aca55e457>>> breaks a shot and cycles the bolt, <<<4f969abd-60d2-4e34-9da2-d933f91e3688>>> fires beside him, brass turning on the concrete between them. CUT TO A LONG LENS DOWN THE LANE: a fighter from <<<image_1>>> mid-zigzag between a wrecked car and a rubble mound stops dead in stride, dust puffing off his chest rig, and goes straight down onto the stones, small and far away. His partner does not go to him and keeps moving.

2.5-5.5s | THE LANE, GROUND LEVEL, LOW AND WIDE — the movement beat: a fighter from <<<image_2>>> breaks out of the alley mouth, cuts hard right, then left, then right again across four paces and DROPS behind the front wheel of a wrecked car, rifle up over the bonnet, head snapping up at the roofline. A second man comes out a beat later on a completely different line, zigzags twice and puts himself behind the burnt-out minibus. A third slices round the corner of a courtyard wall with his shoulder against the render, muzzle leading, one look, gone. Two more bound forward in a pair — one rushes and drops behind the rubble mound, the other passes him at a sprint, changes direction twice and goes down behind the stacked breeze blocks. One is hit as he clears the alley mouth and drops flat two paces out, sliding in the dirt. The rest keep coming, lower, shorter rushes, tighter to the walls.

5.5-8s | THE WINDOW. WIDE, LOW, FROM INSIDE THE GROUND-FLOOR ROOM looking out through a sandbagged window hole: a SEAL is standing at the window hole firing his carbine out into the lane, helmet on, goggles down over his eyes, brass flicking off to one side, sandbags bursting and pouring beside him as rounds come in. AND HE IS HIT. He stops firing mid-burst, comes off the weapon, and goes straight down out of the frame below the sill — the carbine dropping with him. THAT IS THE WHOLE BEAT. Nobody runs to him, nobody drags him, nobody shouts, the camera does not follow him down, and he is not shown on the floor. The window hole he was standing in is simply empty and the dust keeps pouring off the sandbags.

8-12s | SLOW MOTION — JACK IS HIT. Tight, close, low behind the parapet, EXTREME SLOW MOTION, all of it read on him and his kit: <<<93edeb87-e0e7-4ded-9569-527aca55e457>>> is up on his elbows on the rifle when the round arrives in his RIGHT SHOULDER. The impact goes through his body before his face knows about it — the shoulder is driven violently backwards and down, dust and a small burst of torn cloth fibres puff off the top of the shoulder where it strikes, the plate carrier strap snaps taut and jumps, his helmet whips over with the rotation of the torso and the goggle strap pulls tight across the cover. The rifle comes off the bipod and out of his hands, the bolt handle catching the concrete. His right arm goes dead and swings loose. He lands on his side against the parapet with his cheek on the grit, mouth open, breath driven out of him, and for a full beat he does nothing at all — the blankness of a body switched off and switched back on. His eyes stay visible behind the dusty scratched lens the whole time. No blood, no wound, no hole. Empty brass and grit float and turn in the slowed air around him.

12-15.5s | NORMAL SPEED SNAPS BACK — CLOSE ON TERRENCE, and this is his whole beat. He is on the RIGHT of frame; Jack is off his left shoulder on the LEFT of frame.
HE FELT IT BEFORE HE SAW IT. His head comes off the scope and turns toward the LEFT OF FRAME, down to the man lying immediately beside him. His eyes LOCK THERE and do not move — no scanning, no searching, no looking into the distance, no looking up, no looking at the lens. Helmet on, goggles down, the eyes fully readable through the dusty lens. Everything professional goes out of his face in one frame — the mouth opens slightly, the brow goes, and the reaction is plain, human and completely unperformed: this is a man seeing his friend hit.
TERRENCE: "JACK!"
AND HE GOES TO HIM. He pushes up off his rifle onto his forearms and starts to come across the concrete toward Jack — one hand leaving the weapon, one knee coming under him, his whole body committing to the two feet between them.
AND HE DOES NOT GET THERE. A BURST OF ROUNDS SMASHES INTO THE PARAPET RIGHT WHERE HE IS — three or four hits in a line, half a metre from his helmet: chunks blown out of the concrete, a spray of grit and chips straight into his face and across the goggle lens, the wall behind him gouged, dust erupting off the top of the wall. His head snaps down and away, shoulders up over his neck, the whole body flinching flat onto the deck.
He holds there for half a beat with his face in the grit. Then he looks at Jack one more time — a quick, hard, helpless look, two feet away and unreachable — and he ABANDONS IT: he gets back down behind his rifle, jams his cheek onto the stock, and starts firing again. The last thing in the beat is him working the bolt, dust on his goggle lens, jaw set.

15.5-30s | ONE SINGLE UNBROKEN SHOT TO THE END OF THE SCENE — NO CUT ANYWHERE INSIDE THESE FOURTEEN AND A HALF SECONDS. One camera, one setup, one continuous take: a tight close-up, slightly low, <<<93edeb87-e0e7-4ded-9569-527aca55e457>>> propped against the base of the parapet on his good left side, the dead right arm hanging, his rifle on the concrete beside him, dust grey on his face and on the goggle lens, rounds cracking off the wall above his helmet. Terrence stays where he has always been — off to Jack's side, out of focus at the edge of frame or just outside it, firing. THE CAMERA NEVER CUTS, NEVER CHANGES ANGLE AND NEVER RE-FRAMES TO A NEW SETUP — it only breathes and drifts with him, handheld. HIS POSITION AGAINST THE PARAPET DOES NOT CHANGE FROM THE FIRST FRAME OF THIS SHOT TO THE LAST: he does not sit up, does not stand, does not roll over, does not move to another part of the roof, and he is never discovered already holding a radio in a new position. Helmet on, goggles down over his eyes, eyes readable through the lens throughout.
HIS BREATHING RUNS THROUGH THIS ENTIRE TAKE AND NEVER SETTLES: he is BADLY WINDED — hard, fast, ragged breathing, chest pumping, air dragged in through the mouth and pushed back out, the rhythm broken and uneven, a hitch and a catch in it every few breaths, sweat running from under the helmet band. It gets worse across the take, not better. Everything below happens inside this one frame, in this order, with these exact durations.

FIRST — HE LOOKS (15.5-17.5s, two seconds). His head comes down and he LOOKS AT HIS OWN RIGHT SHOULDER, at the torn dusty fabric where the round went in. He does not look at Terrence, not at the lane, not at the lens. He examines it the way you examine something that belongs to someone else, breathing hard the whole time.

SECOND — THE REACTION ARRIVES IN HIS BODY (17.5-19.5s, two seconds, no words at all), involuntary and physical, not acted: a sharp shallow catch of breath sucked in through the teeth; the head tips BACK against the concrete and the eyes screw shut hard behind the lens; the jaw clamps; HIS LEFT HAND COMES ACROSS AND PRESSES FLAT OVER THE SHOULDER AND STAYS THERE; his breathing goes short, fast and shallow through the nose, chest lifting; a shudder runs through him once. He rides it out.

THIRD — THE WORD (19.5-20.5s, one second). The worst of it passes through him, his head comes back down off the wall, his eyes open behind the lens, and he says it on an out-breath — flat, quiet, tired, disgusted, half under his breath, not a shout:
JACK: "Shit!"

FOURTH — THE HAND MOVES (20.5-22s, one and a half seconds), STILL THE SAME SHOT AND THE SAME POSITION, AND THIS IS THE HINGE OF THE TAKE: the LEFT hand — the same hand that has been pressing his shoulder — LIFTS OFF THE WOUND and travels up to the shoulder mic clipped on the left strap of his plate carrier. We see it leave the shoulder and we see it close on the mic. He does not use the right arm, which stays dead and hanging. He does not change how he is lying. The camera stays exactly where it is and simply lets his hand come up into frame. He squeezes the transmit key and takes ONE DEEP RAGGED BREATH before he speaks, and we hear it.

FIFTH — THE RADIO CALL (22-28s, SIX FULL SECONDS FOR TWENTY WORDS — the words are never squeezed into less than six seconds; same unbroken shot, same position, left hand on the mic at his collarbone the whole time). HE IS SHOUTING AND HE IS OUT OF BREATH AT THE SAME TIME, AND THE BREATHLESSNESS IS AS IMPORTANT AS THE VOLUME. Loud, raised, forced, hoarse, straining over the volume of the firefight — but there is not enough air behind it. Each phrase is HAMMERED OUT ON WHATEVER AIR HE HAS, and then he RUNS OUT and has to STOP AND DRAG IN A LOUD RAGGED BREATH THROUGH HIS MOUTH before he can start the next one. The breaths are audible, deep and uneven, and they are what create the gaps between phrases. His voice cracks and thins on the loudest words because it is being pushed past what his lungs have. Fury and urgency under it: teeth showing, the cords standing out in his neck.
BUT THE WORDS THEMSELVES ARE CORRECT, CLEAN AND COMPLETE RADIO PROCEDURE — he never stumbles, never loses the thread, never repeats himself, never mumbles and never says anything unclear. Every word fully formed and hit hard, nothing swallowed, nothing crammed. Loud, breathless and slow at the same time. There are four phrases and he takes a breath before each of the last three.
JACK (shouting into the radio, hoarse and badly out of breath, one short phrase at a time, dragging a loud ragged breath between each):
"All stations, this is Reaper! — We are surrounded! — Taking fire from all four sides! — We need close air support — NOW!"
Behind him, out of focus in the same frame, <<<4f969abd-60d2-4e34-9da2-d933f91e3688>>> is down on his rifle and firing.

SIXTH — THE ANSWER (28-30s, the last two seconds, still the same unbroken shot, same position, left hand still on the mic): hold on his face, chest heaving, still fighting for air, as the radio comes back — thin, compressed and crackling out of a speaker, and by contrast completely calm, unhurried and clearly enunciated:
RADIO (male, calm, American): "Copy, Reaper. Hawk is inbound. Hang tight, boys."
His hand comes off the mic and drops back onto the shoulder. He closes his eyes for half a second behind the lens, breathing still ragged, and that is the only thing his face does. Hold. Last frame.

ACTING TASK — JACK: he is triaging, not suffering. When he looks at the shoulder he is checking a piece of equipment. The reaction that follows is his body overruling him for two seconds, and he lets it pass through rather than fighting it or performing it. "Shit" is irritation at a tool that broke, said quietly because there is nobody he wants to say it to. THEN THE RADIO CALL IS THE OPPOSITE — this is the one moment in the film where he loses his temper, because he has one arm, a man down at the window and forty men closing, and the only thing left that can change the outcome is at the other end of that radio. He is not asking, he is DEMANDING, at full volume. But his body will not cooperate: no air, so every phrase costs him a breath and he has to stop and take it. The words stay correct and procedural anyway, because a man who cannot be understood gets nothing. To make the call he takes the pressure off his own wound and does not hesitate about it for a moment.
ACTING TASK — TERRENCE: for two seconds he stops being a soldier entirely — he is not assessing a casualty and he is not looking for a threat, he is looking at his friend and he is going to him without thinking about it. The burst into the wall is what makes the decision for him, not judgement: his body flinches flat before his mind catches up, and when it does catch up he understands that crossing two feet of concrete will kill him and Jack both. Going back on the rifle is not him recovering his professionalism, it is him giving something up, and the last look he throws at Jack before he does it is the cost.
ACTING TASK — THE FIGHTERS: not suicidal and not extras. Every man is trying to get thirty metres closer without being the next one down — zigzag rushes, proper cover, heads up at the roofline at every stop; when the man beside them goes down they do not stop, they change their line.

SOUND: two bolt-actions and carbines working, AK fire from four directions cracking off concrete, rounds hitting sandbags and stone, brass on the deck, Pashto passed lane to lane. Under the SLOW MOTION beat the mix drops to a muffled underwater roar with the impact itself almost dry and small, then a thin ringing. Normal speed returns with Terrence's shout. The burst into the parapet beside him is four hard cracks and the spatter of concrete chips, very close on the mic. SCENE: the rooftop, mid-battle after the car-bomb. Jack and Terrence are pinned behind the parapet; a large force of Taliban fighters is closing on the building from cover to cover. Jack is shot in the right shoulder and calls in an air strike. Terrence hears it and understands what it will cost — but says nothing, because he is fighting for their lives. Below, civilians hear the jets and scramble for cover.

BLOCKING: Jack (A) and Terrence (B) prone behind the rooftop parapet, side by side. Down the long street, ~30 Taliban fighters in civilian clothes and headscarves advance in bounding overwatch — rushing cover to cover, some on distant rooftops — closing steadily on the building. In the alleys and doorways below, Afghan civilians.

ACTION (28s):
0–4s: Jack rises to fire over the parapet — and is HIT in the RIGHT SHOULDER, his firing shoulder, where the rifle stock is seated. SLOW MOTION: the round strikes, his body twists with the impact, his face contorting, the rifle jolting from his grip, dust and grit kicking off the parapet beside him, spent brass hanging in the golden air. His helmet tips, his mouth opens in a cry lost under the ringing. Time stretched, brutal, silent but for tinnitus.
4–8s: BACK TO REAL TIME — Jack slides down behind the parapet into cover, back against the low wall, right arm hanging useless, his left hand clamping the ruined right shoulder, teeth bared, breathing hard and ragged. Rounds crack overhead, chewing the top of the parapet.
TERRENCE (shouting, turning): "JACK!"
He reaches toward Jack — but a burst rakes the parapet right at him, forcing him back onto his rifle. He can't go to Jack. He has to fight.
8–13s: Terrence stays on the gun, working the bolt, firing down the street in disciplined shots — TIGHT ON TERRENCE'S FACE, jaw set, eyes hard, cycling and firing, holding the wall alone. WIDE DOWN THE STREET: the Taliban fighters bound closer from cover to cover, muzzle flashes winking from behind cars and doorways and distant rooftops — too many, closing in. The two of them are badly outnumbered.
13–20s: Jack, slumped in cover against the parapet, drags his radio handset up with his good LEFT hand, his right arm limp at his side. His voice is strained now, breath short and uneven, the wound pulling at every word:
JACK (radio, strained, breathing hard): "Hawk... ground element — we are surrounded, danger close... need air support on this street — now, bring it in NOW."
RADIO VOICE (through static, calm): "Copy ground element — birds inbound. Hold on."
Beside him Terrence keeps firing — but at Jack's words his eyes flick sideways for a fraction of a second. HE HEARS IT. A flicker crosses his face — he knows what an air strike on this street will do, how many will die down there. But he says nothing. He turns back to his scope and keeps fighting, jaw tightening — no time, no choice.
20–24s: BELOW, in the alleys and doorways — civilians hear the rising jets. A mother pulls a child indoors, a knot of people scatter from a doorway, an old man hurries others back, faces turning up to the sky, everyone breaking for cover in dawning panic. Ordinary life bolting from a sound it knows.
24–28s: back on the roof — the roar of jets swelling now, close. Jack, pale, breathing hard, slumped against the parapet, left hand still clamped over his ruined right shoulder, stares up toward the sound of what he's called in. Terrence fires one more disciplined burst, then his eyes lift too — both men, for one held beat, looking up as the roar becomes deafening. Hold on their two faces, the incoming howl filling everything. Cut.

CAMERA: action grammar — wide close handheld. The shoulder hit in stark slow motion — impact, twist, brass in the air, then a hard snap back to real-time chaos. Low behind the parapet with Jack sliding into cover. Tight on Terrence's face firing, and the small sideways flick of his eyes when he hears the radio call — the key beat. Wide down the street on the closing fighters. A drop below to the civilians scattering. The end tilts up with both men toward the jet roar. Horizon tilts throughout, tinnitus-muffled world.

ACTING TASK:
Jack — motive: the machine that does what must be done. Goal: save what's left of his team. Obstacle: the right shoulder wound — his firing arm is finished, the ragged breath, the pain pulling at his voice. Tactic: he blocks the pain out enough to work the radio one-handed with his good left arm; calling the strike is pure procedure — he does not let himself think about the street below, only the threat. The breath is short, the words are steady.
Terrence — motive: cover his partner, hold the wall. Goal: keep the fighters off the roof, keep Jack alive. Obstacle: he can't go to Jack, and he can hear what Jack is calling in. Tactic: he fights — but the flick of his eyes at Jack's radio call is everything: he understands the cost in that instant, and he swallows it, because he has a rifle in his hands and thirty men closing and no time to argue. He says nothing. The knowing lives in his face, not his mouth.
Safety line: gazes engaged in the task, natural blinking; pain and knowing read as function, not melodrama.

SOUND: high ringing tinnitus over everything. The shoulder hit near-silent in slow motion but for the ring and a low impact thud. Then real-time: incoming fire cracking off the parapet, Terrence's rifle cycling and firing, brass, Terrence's shout "JACK!". Jack's strained, breath-short radio call; the calm reply through static. Below, the civilians' panic — sandals, shouts, a child. Then, rising and swelling underneath, the roar of approaching jets, building to deafening. No music.

FORBIDDEN: US soldiers never fire on each other; every US soldier in helmet and ballistic goggles; long guns sand-coloured; the shoulder hit shows impact, twist and pain but no gore, no open wound detail beyond the clamped shoulder; fighters shown only as distant advancing figures and muzzle flashes; civilians shown only running and scattering, never harmed; no subtitles, no music.

ACTING TASK — TERRENCE: from the moment the boy puts his hands on that launcher, Terrence is not frozen and he is not afraid — he is REFUSING. He keeps hunting for any version of the next ten seconds that does not require him to do it: a warning shot, a shout, somebody else, the boy losing his nerve, the tube being too heavy. Underneath it he is stuck on one fact he cannot put down — that this boy is doing exactly what any of them would do, and that the thing the boy is avenging is the call his own team made. He knows precisely what his refusal will cost and he refuses anyway.
ACTING TASK — JACK: he is protecting seven men with one working arm and no time, and he does the thing nobody else will. The screaming is not rage at Terrence, it is a man trying to get a job done through somebody who has stopped working. The look he gives him afterwards is not contempt — it is a man handing somebody else a bill he has decided to pay himself.
ACTING TASK — THE BOY: he is not a fighter and never becomes one. He is a child doing the only thing he can think of, badly — the launcher is too heavy, his hands are wrong on it, he is still crying while he lifts it. Nothing about him is competent and nothing about him is menacing except the direction the tube is pointing.

SCENE: the rooftop, mid-battle after the car-bomb. Jack and Terrence are pinned behind the parapet; ~30 Taliban fighters close from cover to cover down the street. Jack, shot in the right shoulder, calls in an air strike. Through his scope Terrence sees civilians down the street and tries to stop him — but Jack calls it in anyway.

BLOCKING — read the geometry carefully: Jack (A) and Terrence (B) lie prone side by side behind the same rooftop parapet, TERRENCE ON JACK'S LEFT (Terrence to frame-left, Jack to his right), both facing the SAME direction — out over the parapet and straight DOWN THE LONG STREET where the Taliban are advancing. Both rifles point down that street at the far advancing fighters. Neither man ever turns his rifle away from the street; all their fire goes toward the advancing Taliban down the length of the road. Further down that same street and in its side-alleys, Afghan civilians — families, children — are caught in the open, scattering.

ACTION (30s):
0–4s: Jack rises to fire over the parapet — and is HIT in the RIGHT SHOULDER, his firing shoulder, where the stock is seated. SLOW MOTION: the round strikes, his body twists, face contorting, the rifle jolting from his grip, brass hanging in the golden air, his helmet tipping, his mouth open in a cry lost under the ringing. Brutal, stretched, silent but for tinnitus.
4–8s: REAL TIME — Jack slides down behind the parapet into cover, back to the wall, right arm hanging useless, left hand clamping the ruined right shoulder, breathing hard and ragged. Rounds chew the parapet overhead.
TERRENCE (shouting, turning his head to his right toward Jack): "JACK!"
He reaches toward Jack with one hand — but a burst rakes the parapet, forcing him back onto his rifle. He can't reach him. He swings back to face down the street and fights.
8–13s: Terrence, on Jack's LEFT, stays on his rifle behind the parapet, firing DOWN THE STREET at the advancing Taliban — never turning away from that direction, always shooting toward the far end of the road where the fighters bound from cover to cover. TIGHT ON TERRENCE'S FACE, jaw set, eyes hard, cycling the bolt and firing down the street, holding the wall alone. WIDE FROM BEHIND THE TWO MEN, over their shoulders and down the long street: the Taliban fighters advancing toward the building, muzzle flashes winking from cars, doorways and distant rooftops — Terrence's and Jack's fire going out toward them down the road. Badly outnumbered.
13–17s: Jack drags the radio up with his good left hand and keys it, voice strained, breath short:
JACK (radio, strained): "Hawk, this is ground element — we are surrounded, danger close, request immediate air support—"
17–22s: Terrence, still firing down the street, sweeps his scope along the far end to range the threat — and through the glass he SEES them: past the advancing fighters, further down the street and spilling from the side-alleys, CIVILIANS in the open — women, a knot of children, families running. THROUGH TERRENCE'S SCOPE: small distant figures of civilians scattering in panic down the road. His head jerks up off the scope, turning to his right toward Jack, alarmed:
TERRENCE (shouting): "Jack — there's civilians down there — a lot of them, families, kids—!"
22–26s: Jack doesn't look down the street. He doesn't answer the word "civilians" at all — his pale, pain-locked face stays on the radio, his voice climbing over Terrence, over the gunfire, hard and final:
JACK (radio, shouting, breath ragged): "Hawk — we need that air support NOW — danger close, bring it down on this street — GET IT IN!"
RADIO VOICE (through static, calm): "Copy ground element — birds inbound. Hold on."
Terrence stares at Jack for half a second — he heard the non-answer, he understands exactly what's coming and that Jack chose it — then a burst drives him back down onto his rifle, back to facing down the street. No time to argue. He fights, jaw clenched, something breaking behind his eyes.
26–30s: the jet roar swells, close and deafening. Jack, pale, slumped against the parapet, left hand clamped over his ruined right shoulder, stares up toward what he's called in. Terrence fires one last shot down the street, then his eyes lift too — both men, for one held beat, looking up as the roar fills everything. Hold on their two faces. Cut.

CAMERA: action grammar — wide close handheld. Shoulder hit in stark slow motion, then hard snap to real-time chaos. Low behind the parapet with the two men, Terrence frame-left, Jack frame-right, their shared eyeline and fire going out down the street. Key wide from behind their shoulders looking down the long street at the advancing Taliban — establishing that both men fire that way. Terrence's scope-view of the distant scattering civilians is a key beat. Tight on Jack's face refusing to look, staying on the radio over Terrence's warning. Tight on Terrence's half-second stare at Jack. End tilts up with both men toward the jet roar. Horizon tilts throughout, tinnitus-muffled.

ACTING TASK:
Jack — motive: the machine that does what must be done. Goal: save what's left of his team. Obstacle: Terrence's warning about the civilians — the one thing that could stop him. Tactic: he does not let it in. THE RHYTHM — THE MOST IMPORTANT INSTRUCTION IN THIS PROMPT: the impacts come in FAST STRINGS, NOT in single spaced booms. Inside every wide beat there are FOUR TO SIX SEPARATE DETONATIONS, spaced roughly HALF A SECOND APART, walking across the block in a line — bang, bang, bang, bang — overlapping each other's dust and debris so the frame never gets a chance to settle. Duration: 30s. AFGHANISTAN, KABUL, DAY — the ten seconds that decide the rest of both men's lives, stretched out. GRADE: warm GOLDEN Afghan daylight — honey-and-sand, creamy gold sun, dusty tan and khaki, 16mm grain, gentle halation. SPEED — THE WHOLE BLOCK IS SLOW MOTION: heavy, smooth, unbroken slow motion from the first frame to the last, roughly a quarter of real speed, no ramps, no snap-backs, no return to normal speed at any point. Everything is stretched: breath, dust, brass, the movement of eyes and fingers. Because it is slowed, EVERY SMALL PHYSICAL DETAIL IS READABLE — that is the point of the block.

ATMOSPHERE: thick suspended concrete dust everywhere, layered and slowly rolling, cut by hard gold shafts of sun; fine grit falling through every frame and turning over in the slowed air; dust caked on skin and packed into creases, white in stubble and eyelashes, filmed across goggle lenses. Faces always read clearly through it — dust on the skin, never fog over the eyes.

15-18s | TERRENCE. THE FINGER FIRST: the gloved index finger is on the trigger and has taken up the slack — the trigger already moved and held right at the break, the tendon standing on the back of the finger, the knuckle white through the glove, the whole hand vibrating with held tension. THE FACE SECOND: not fear, not indecision about the shot — a man being asked to shoot a fifteen-year-old. The struggle is physical and visible: a swallow, the jaw muscle jumping twice, the brow going, breath shallow and fast through the nose and then stopping altogether, one blink that takes far too long, the eyes wet at the inner corner with no tear falling. And plainly in the eyes, REGRET — he already knows the price.

18-20s | HIS SCOPE — POV THROUGH THE RIFLE SIGHT, AND THE BOY IS IN IT. A circular field with a soft dark vignette at the edges, the glass dusty and scratched, a simple fine black reticle across it. He sits exactly where the reticle sits. The image breathes very slightly with Terrence's breath and then goes completely still as the breath stops. Two seconds of holding him there and doing nothing.

20-21.5s | BACK ON TERRENCE, TIGHT: THE FINGER COMES OFF THE TRIGGER. It lifts slowly and deliberately and lays itself flat along the outside of the trigger guard. He does not lower the rifle and he does not look away from the scope. He simply stops being able to use it. One long exhale moves the dust in front of his mouth.

21.5-23s | THE BOY'S POINT OF VIEW, THROUGH THE LAUNCHER'S OPTICAL SIGHT: a small dirty rectangular window with a simple crude etched grid across it, glass scratched and dust-filmed, edges black and soft. Through it, thirty metres away and level, the American parapet and behind it the two dusty tan helmets and shoulders. The sight drifts and wobbles — the tube is too heavy for him and will not hold still — swings past them, comes back, and settles. His breathing rocks the frame.

23-26.5s | JACK BARELY GETS THE RIFLE UP — THREE AND A HALF SECONDS OF PURE PHYSICAL STRUGGLE, MEDIUM THEN TIGHTER, and it must look like it costs him everything. His LEFT hand comes off the concrete and gropes down for the rifle lying on the deck. He gets it by the tan handguard and LIFTS — and it is nearly too much for one arm: the muzzle comes up first and the butt drags on the concrete, the whole weapon swinging and tipping in his single grip, the bipod legs catching on the parapet edge and snagging, dust dragging off it in slow sheets. He gets the forend up onto the capping, loses it a few centimetres, catches it again with the heel of his hand, and finally SHOVES it into place across the top of the parapet so the concrete takes all its weight. His breath comes in short hard bursts. The right arm hangs and swings and contributes nothing.

26.5-29.5s | THE LEFT-HANDED SHOT — TIGHT CLOSE, AND THE AWKWARDNESS IS THE WHOLE POINT. He has to shoot the rifle from the wrong side, off the WRONG SHOULDER, because his right shoulder cannot take the recoil at all. Every detail of that wrongness is readable in the slow motion:
— HE PULLS THE BUTT INTO HIS LEFT SHOULDER, not the right, wedging it into the plate carrier on the left side and pinning it there with the weight of his upper body.
— HIS LEFT HAND CLOSES ROUND THE GRIP the wrong way and his LEFT INDEX FINGER goes inside the trigger guard, the wrist bent at an ugly angle to make it reach.
— HE HAS NO SECOND HAND FOR THE FOREND — nothing supports the front of the rifle but the concrete, so he presses down on the parapet with his chest to steady it instead.
— HIS HEAD IS ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE STOCK: he has to crane his neck over the top of the receiver and tip his head to get his LEFT eye behind the scope, the cheek rest under the wrong cheek, the goggle frame jamming against the rubber eyecup, his shoulder hunched up around his ear.
— THE BOLT HANDLE AND THE EJECTION PORT ARE NOW ON THE FAR SIDE, facing away from his hand, unreachable — he has one shot and no way to work the action.
— HE FIGHTS FOR THE SIGHT PICTURE: the eye behind the lens searching, the head shifting twice, the rifle sliding a centimetre on the dusty concrete and being dragged back.
Then he settles. The breath goes out of him in one long slow stream that stirs the dust on the capping, and then there is no breath at all. Absolute stillness for half a second. THE SHOT: a single sharp recoil rolling back into his LEFT shoulder, the butt driving into the carrier, the rifle jumping on the concrete and skating sideways out of his one-handed grip, the empty case turning over slowly in the air, a ring of dust lifting off the parapet. His face closes at once — and his RIGHT shoulder jolts with the shock through his body, and that is where the pain lands even though the recoil went into the other side.

29.5-30s | HOLD on his face for the last half second. The far building and the boy are NOT in frame from 23s onward and nothing is shown of what the shot does. Last frame.

ACTING TASK — JACK: he is not angry at Terrence and he is not brave. He is doing arithmetic with one arm and no time, and the scream is the sound of a man trying to make somebody else's hands work. When they do not, he does it himself — and the last four seconds are not heroic, they are clumsy, laboured and undignified, a man fighting his own equipment with half a body, because the alternative is watching seven men die for a decision nobody made.
ACTING TASK — TERRENCE: he is not frozen and not afraid. He is REFUSING, and losing something while he does it. It is all in the hand and the eyes: the trigger already at the break, the tension held far too long, the boy sitting in his reticle for two full seconds, and then the deliberate act of taking the finger off — a decision, not a failure of nerve. The regret is not only about the boy; it is about knowing exactly what he is handing to the man beside him.
ACTING TASK — THE BOY: fifteen, and doing it badly. The tube is too heavy, his sight will not hold still, he is breathing in gulps. Not menacing, not competent — only pointing.

SOUND: everything stretched, low and thick under the slow motion. Dust falling and settling, small fires far off, a long high ringing tone under all of it. Jack's breath dragged out deep and wet, the scrape of his kit on concrete, the rifle grinding and knocking on the stone, the slow rasp of his glove on the handguard, the butt thudding into his carrier. Terrence's breath shallow and fast, then nothing. The scream comes through slowed, deep and warped. Under the boy's POV, only his own breathing and the wobble of the sight. One shot, flattened and dragged, and the rifle skating on concrete after it. No music.

ACTING TASK — THE BOY: fifteen, no longer uncertain; not menacing, not competent — the grip too big for his hand — but decided, and the decision sits in that finger.

Jack and Terrence sit side by side resting in the shade near the mouth of a long mud-brick passage — kit loosened, helmets off beside them, rifles leaned aside. Terrence keeps looking at a small ultrasound photo; Jack ribs him about it. A warm, easy moment between two friends — the calm the whole tragedy is measured against. Duration: 12s. THIS IS A NIGHT SCENE — 2 A.M., THE HARDEST RULE, IT OVERRIDES EVERYTHING. No sun, no sky detail, no daylight, no dusk, no dawn, no blue hour, no day-for-night. Every frame dark: about ninety percent of the picture is pure black with zero detail, built only from two or three small pools of light with hard black between them, the men readable only when they stand in one. Underexpose two stops.
NAME EVERY SOURCE, NO OTHERS: (1) two sodium street lamps far away at the mouth of the alley, always OUT OF FRAME — dirty greenish-yellow light arriving weak, low, almost horizontal, throwing long thin pools on the wet concrete and dying before the back wall; (2) a couple of tiny warm windows high up on a neighbouring building, deep background, out of focus. Nothing else emits light: no yard lamp, no work light, no floodlight, no torch, no phone, no headlights, no top light, no fill, no moon.
LOCATION — THE BACK YARD OF THE BUILDING UNDER RENOVATION: a narrow rear service yard between the back wall of the empty walk-up and the blank brick flank of the next building, ~5 metres across, opening at one end into a dark alley to the street. Cracked concrete, standing puddles, plaster crumbs, a dented steel dumpster of renovation debris, plywood sheets, scaffold poles, a wheelbarrow on its side, orange cable, a rusted standpipe; a black iron fire escape up the back wall past polythene-covered openings; a rusted steel site door two steps up; a sagging chain-link gate at the alley end. Everything black except what the distant lamps reach.
GRADE: Fight Club night grade, exactly David Fincher and DP Jeff Cronenweth — dirty sodium greenish-yellow highlights, grimy green-teal shadows, crushed murky blacks with no lift, low saturation, pale greenish skin, fine film grain.

CHARACTERS: JACK <<<cd7d691a-d4f5-46ca-920c-00b72c36ebee>>> — lean man ~45 in a black knitted wool balaclava with THREE holes (two eyes, one mouth), black hooded windbreaker, black gloves, the rifle case <<<f8f36d9d-eb84-4417-9cc2-1e85499ff799>>> slung tight on his back on two straps. TERRENCE <<<d9aeaf90-db99-4c74-8606-a13730f3c54f>>> — his target, standing in the yard with a black pistol.

JACK stands where he stopped, two steps down into the yard, the case on his back, masked — only his eyes in the holes catching a thin greenish rake of lamplight, the rest of him black. Two steps ahead, blocking the way to the alley, TERRENCE stands planted in a locked two-handed stance, black pistol raised level at Jack, side-lit, his far side black. Both still. Breath between them.
4-8s | JACK REACHES TO UNMASK — SAYING NOTHING. Slowly, deliberately, Jack lifts one gloved hand toward his own head and takes hold of the edge of the balaclava — he is going to pull it off, to show his face, to be known. He says nothing at all; the whole act is silent, calm, almost gentle, his eyes steady on Terrence over the raised pistol. The hand starts to draw the wool up.
8-12s | TERRENCE FIRES — FRONTAL, INTO THE LENS. HARD CUT to TERRENCE seen FRONTALLY, straight on, the camera where Jack is — Terrence facing us, pistol raised dead at the lens, side-lit greenish, his far side black, his eyes cold and reading, no hesitation. He FIRES: ONE muzzle flash blooming at the pistol straight toward camera, the recoil kicking his hands, the report cracking the silence — and on the flash the frame CUTS HARD TO BLACK. We never see the bullet reach Jack, never see Jack hit, never see him fall — the image ends on Terrence firing into the lens and the black that swallows it. Hold black.

ACTING TASK — JACK: no fear, no plea, no words. He reaches to take the mask off because he wants the last thing to be true — he wants his friend to see him, to know. It is calm, almost peaceful, a man choosing to be known at the end. He never rushes it; the hand moves slow and sure.
ACTING TASK — TERRENCE: he got here first and he does what he was taught long ago — he does not hesitate, he does not wait to see a face, he takes the shot the instant the target's hand moves. His eyes are cold and certain, reading the movement as a threat, firing on it. No flicker of doubt, no recognition — he shoots a masked man reaching, and never knows who it was. He shoots first, exactly as he was once told to.

SOUND: distant city hum, two men breathing in a closed yard, the tiny drag of wool as Jack's glove takes the mask edge — then ONE hard pistol report into the lens, and dead silence over black. No music.

SCENE — MEMORY FLASHBACK. Daytime, an old-style American diner. The camera is OUTSIDE on the street, looking through the shopfront window at JACK in the window booth: he lowers his hand from his wrist and gazes out at the street. A waitress steps to the table and asks what he wants; he doesn't look at her, only says "the usual"; she doesn't write anything, she asks him to be specific — only then does he pull his gaze back, breathe out, and turn to face her. The camera cuts inside; he gives the order: coffee, apple pie, check all at once. She writes it down and turns away. The whole scene is only the ordering — no food is ever served.

STYLE — the grammar of memory: dreamlike heavy soft focus, edges melting, highlights blooming into ovals, motion carrying a very light trail. Daytime grade is a Killer-style murky olive-green and sulphur-yellow, underexposed about 1.5 stops, the image living in the upper shadows; the daylight through the window is the only motivated source, big and soft; blacks deep but keeping texture; skin natural and warm — the murky green-yellow stays on the environment, the china and the glass, and never lands on the face. Clean air, no floating particles.

CAMERA & LENS: RED Gemini, custom Leica lenses with a low-contrast filter, no harsh highlights. Vintage 2x anamorphic: oval-stretched bokeh, cat-eye flares at the frame edges, out-of-focus highlights smeared into horizontal ovals, subtle chromatic aberration, low-saturation restrained colour. All movement is motorized mechanical movement — dolly and mechanical orbit, perfectly even and very slow, with gentle cushioned starts and stops, absolutely precise paths; never handheld, never shaky. Focus changes are manual rack-focus with a clear start and end point. No lens glare, no light streaks; straight lines at the frame edge stay straight.

This scene he wears a charcoal-grey hooded sweatshirt under a dark work jacket, no gloves. @loc_SNP_diner — old-style American diner booth area and the street-facing shopfront window. THE WAITRESS: about 50, an ordinary warm American diner waitress, pale apron, hair pinned up, holding an order pad and pencil, with the real professional smile she gives every customer. The reference images control only appearance and scene identity, not the brightness or grade of the image.

FIRST FRAME & STAGING: the camera is outside on the street, through the shopfront glass. Jack's face fills centre-left of frame, a big close-up, through a layer of glass; the brick wall across the street, bare branches and parked cars are superimposed as reflections on the glass, lying gently over his face — but his eyes stay clearly readable, never washed out by the reflection. The right of frame is the depth of the diner, empty for now. His left hand is just falling from his right wrist.

FORMAT: two shots, 20 seconds total. Shot 1 runs 10.5 seconds with no cut. Memory soft focus throughout. All dialogue in English.

ACTION TIMELINE:
SHOT 1 — 0.0 to 10.5s — [camera outside, through glass, extremely slow even push-in, no cut throughout]
0.0–2.2s: Jack lowers his left hand from his right wrist back onto the table edge, gaze going past the camera out to the street, motionless. A car passes on the street, its reflection sweeping horizontally across his face and away. In the depth at frame right, the waitress steps to the table and stops, soft-focus through the glass — only her outline and the pale of her apron.
2.2–3.8s: LINE: "What can I get you?"
3.8–5.8s: he doesn't move, doesn't turn, eyes still on the street. LINE, flat, almost no lip movement: "The usual."
5.8–7.6s: her hand doesn't move, the pencil doesn't drop. The line comes right back: "You'll have to be more specific."
7.6–10.5s: his gaze pulls back from the depth of the street to inside — the camera still pushing in; he breathes out, his shoulders settling; then he slowly turns his head to face her at frame right, his face turning out of the reflection-covered zone and becoming fully clear. The push-in stops.
CUT AT 10.5s
SHOT 2 — 10.5 to 20.0s — back inside, framing up from over her shoulder, the camera moving along a mechanical arc extremely slowly around her shoulder toward Jack: his gaze rests on the pencil tip, delivery flat, no weight between the three things — "Coffee. Apple pie. And the check right away." Only now the pencil drops to the pad, scoring three lines. As the orbit ends her shoulder slides out of frame, leaving only him; rack-focus travels from the pencil tip to his eyes. She turns and leaves; he hands his gaze back to the street. Hold one beat, cut to black.

ACTING TASK (the work is in the eyes, do not act emotion):
Scene direction (the shared unspoken direction for both): play these twenty seconds as an ordinary order.
Scene event: a service — one person being served, one person serving.
JACK — motive: this ritual is the one part of the job he doesn't get to choose; it stopped meaning anything long ago, it's just a queue he has to stand in again each time. Goal: get through it with the fewest possible moves, leaving no one a reason to remember him. Obstacle: the process makes him say the words out loud while she waits there with her smile; the moment impatience shows, he becomes a customer who gets remembered. Tactic: through all of Shot 1 he gives his attention to the street — he watches the cars, the door across the way, who passes; a habit built over years, the eyes always working, never going blank; he doesn't turn when she speaks because not-turning itself makes the exchange end faster; "the usual" is said to the glass, not to a person; the instant he hears "more specific" he knows he miscalculated — his gaze pulls back from the street to the room for the first time, the one moment this scene forces him back to this table; the breath is a queuing man's breath, not a dangerous man's — that breath is this scene's delivery; after he turns he looks at the pencil tip, not her eyes; the moment he finishes he hands his gaze back to the street, like returning something borrowed.
THE WAITRESS — motive: the shift is normal, this is a quiet customer; she asks him to be specific because she simply doesn't remember him — which is exactly what he has spent years wanting. Goal: get the order right, don't hold up this table. Tactic: her smile is the one she gives everyone; "the usual" means nothing to her, so she doesn't even lift the pencil, she just asks for a word she can write; once she has it, the pencil drops easily and she turns away briskly.
(Safety line: both keep their eyes engaged in their own task, never dead or glazed, never blank staring; a natural blink rhythm — especially in Shot 1's long stillness there must be real breathing and blinking.)

PHYSICS: the shopfront glass has real thickness and slight unevenness, the reflection slowly warping and shifting as the camera pushes in; when the car passes its reflection slides horizontally along the glass; the hand falling from the wrist has real weight and a pause; the pencil meets the paper with slight resistance and the stroke advances; the apron fabric lags with inertia as she turns. Any motion trail follows the camera and character movement direction only, producing no extra shake and no smearing on the image itself.

SOUND: everyday diner room tone, muffled as if under a layer of water: cutlery clinking, espresso-machine steam, faint voices, a door bell once. Shot 1, being shot from the street, carries a slight through-glass muffling and mixes in street tone — a car passing, a distant horn. Dialogue clear and up front; Jack's breath clearly audible. No music, no narration, no extra dialogue; lips still when not speaking.

SHOT 1 — 0.0 to 10.5s — [camera outside, through glass, extremely slow even push-in, no cut]
0.0–2.2s: Jack lowers his left hand from his right wrist back onto the table edge, gaze going past the camera out to the street, motionless, deep in his own thoughts — somewhere far away. A car passes, its reflection sweeping horizontally across the glass beside him, not across his face. In the depth at frame right, the waitress steps to the table and stops, soft-focus through the glass — outline and the pale of her apron.
2.2–3.8s: LINE (warm, familiar): "What can I get you?"
3.8–5.5s: he doesn't move, doesn't turn, eyes still on the street, still half-lost in thought. LINE, TIRED and low, worn out, almost no lip movement, said to the glass not to her: "The usual."
5.5–7.8s: a small beat — she knows him, knows what he means, but she can't take it; it has to be said in full. Gently, a touch apologetic, but firm: "I'm sorry, hon. I still need the whole order."
7.8–10.5s: his gaze pulls back from the street to inside — camera still pushing in; he breathes out, shoulders settling; then he slowly turns his head to face her at frame right, face clean and fully readable, the eyes going cold and a little hard as they land on her. The push-in stops.
CUT AT 10.5s
SHOT 2 — 10.5 to 20.0s — inside, framing up from over her shoulder, camera on a mechanical arc extremely slowly around her shoulder toward Jack: he looks STRAIGHT AT HER — not down, no notepad, nothing in her hands — his eyes cold and level on her, and gives it flat and exact, each item its own beat, like a passphrase: "Black coffee. Apple pie, warmed. And the check — all at once." She just takes it in, a small knowing nod, nothing written. As the orbit ends her shoulder slides out of frame, leaving only him; rack-focus settles on his eyes. She turns and leaves; he hands his gaze back to the street. Hold one beat, cut to black.

ACTING TASK (the work is in the eyes, do not act emotion):
Scene direction (shared, unspoken): play these twenty seconds as an exchange that looks like an order but is a passphrase — both know it, neither says so, and nothing is written down.
JACK — motive: the ritual is the one part of the job he doesn't choose; say the words, get out. He is deep in his own head when it starts — the "the usual" comes out tired and worn, thrown to the glass, a man who has done this too many times. Obstacle: she makes him say it in full, which pulls him out of his thoughts and back to the table — the one thing he didn't want. Tactic: when he turns to her he doesn't soften — the eyes go cold and a little hard, faintly annoyed at being made to perform the ritual; he says the passphrase straight into her face, level and exact, holding her eyes, not looking away, not looking down — there is nothing to look down at. The instant it's done he hands his gaze back to the street.
THE WAITRESS — motive: she knows exactly who he is and what this is — but the rule is the rule, it has to be spoken in full; she won't cut the corner, even for him. She has nothing to write and doesn't pretend to; the warmth and the small "I'm sorry, hon" are real and also cover. Her eyes hold a half-second of knowing on him; once he says it in full, a small nod, and she's gone.
(Safety line: both keep eyes engaged in the task, never dead or glazed; natural blink and real breathing, especially in Shot 1's long stillness.)

Motion trail follows camera and environment only, stays off the face, no extra shake, no smearing on the image.

Shot 1, from the street, carries slight through-glass muffling and street tone — a car passing, a distant horn. Dialogue clear and up front; Jack's first line tired and worn, his breath audible; his order flat and cold; her small apologetic line warm and low. No music, no narration, no extra dialogue; lips still when not speaking.

记忆的语法:整段梦境般浓重柔焦——边缘融化、高光晕成椭圆、动作带极轻拖影;碎片之间生硬闪切,部分切口带一帧近白闪光。咖啡馆白天是《杀手》式浑浊橄榄绿与硫磺黄。夜景是浓烈芬奇色谱:病态荧光绿(洗车机顶灯、地铁站台灯管)与刺目红(尾灯、出口标志)在湿夜里互相渗透。整体欠曝一档半,画面活在阴影上部;黑位深沉但保留质感;肤色始终自然温暖,浑浊的绿黄留在环境里,不落在脸上。

摄影机与镜头

RED Gemini,Leica定制镜头加低反差滤镜,无刺眼高光。复古2倍变形宽银幕:椭圆拉伸焦外,画面边缘猫眼光斑,失焦高光抹成水平长椭圆,轻微色差,低饱和克制色彩。运动一律为电动机械运动——微距下移、滑轨、缓慢推近,匀速精确,绝不手持抖动。无镜头眩光,无光线拉丝,画面边缘直线保持笔直。

表演任务(功课在眼里,不演情绪)

杰克——

动机:这不是一场对抗,是一道工序;工序里没有对手,只有工件。

目标:在窗口时间内确认并完成,不让任何多余的东西进入他的注意力。

战术:跟踪时他看的是对方的步幅、口袋的位置、身边有没有第二个人,眼睛始终在采集信息、绝不放空;执行的两个瞬间,他的目光只做一件事——核对:是这个人、位置对、时间对;对方的恐惧对他而言是画面里的天气,不是信息,所以他的脸对此毫无反应,眼睛不躲、不多看一秒。

两名目标——

战术:直到最后一刻他们都还在用日常的逻辑理解眼前的事;真正的恐惧发生在"这解释不通"的那半秒里——他们看的不是凶器,是杰克的眼睛,并且在里面找不到任何可以谈判的东西;身体先于头脑往后退。

(安全线:所有人目光始终投入各自的任务,绝不僵死呆滞、绝不空洞发直;自然眨眼节奏。)

Medium-format commercial fitting photography, 100mm equivalent prime, camera at chest height, frame absolutely level. The whole image is one real studio photograph — not a collage, not an illustration layout.

Anime, illustration look, painterly look, 3D render, CGI texture, airbrushed skin, plastic skin, waxwork, oversaturated HDR, lens flare, horizontal light streaks, starburst, halo bloom, bright areas washing out and losing detail; any scar, cut or mark on the face; any text, annotation lines, arrows, colour charts, labels or watermarks in the frame.

Straight-on product photograph of a single paper shooting target pinned flat against a plain neutral dark grey backdrop, shot square to the surface with no perspective and no tilt, the target centred and filling most of the frame.

The target is a classic printed range target on off-white matte paper with a faint cream tone and a slightly rough fibrous texture. On it, TEN CONCENTRIC CIRCLES perfectly centred inside one another, printed in thin clean black line-work, evenly spaced from the outer edge to the middle.

The scoring rings are NUMBERED FROM 1 TO 10 FROM THE OUTSIDE IN: the widest outer ring is marked "1", each ring inwards counts up — 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 — and the very centre is the 10. Each number is printed in a simple bold black sans-serif, repeated at the top, bottom, left and right of its own ring so the figures sit on the vertical and horizontal axes.

THE CENTRE, THE TEN, IS A SOLID BLACK FILLED DISC — completely opaque matte black, no ring outline inside it, no number printed on it, no white gap, roughly one fifth of the width of the whole target. Every other ring is unfilled white paper with only the printed black outlines and numbers on it.

A thin black cross of fine aiming lines runs vertically and horizontally through the centre of the target, and the paper shows honest wear: soft creases, a slightly bent corner, four small pin holes at the corners, a little dust and shadowing at the edges.

Even soft frontal studio light with a gentle falloff to the corners, no glare on the paper, no reflections, no hotspots. Crisp photographic detail, real paper fibre, subtle desaturated cool grade, fine film grain, deep neutral background with no texture and no props. They move to their spots and set up — Jack and Terrence drop prone behind the parapet, extending bipods, settling the rifles onto the low wall, cheeks to stocks, scoping down the long golden street; C and D setting up below.
